slides.title: A powerful AI does not necessarily help learning
slides.navigationLabel: A powerful AI does not necessarily help learning
slides.source: Bastani et al. (2025); Kosmyna et al. (2025); Stadler et al. (2024); Tao, Mathematics in the Age of AI (2026)
slides.text:
1 · WHY CHANGE 03a
A powerful AI does not necessarily help learning
Multiple studies showed that learning with access to AI may
lead to worse independent test performance (i.e., without
AI).
• Bastani et al., “Generative AI without guardrails can harm
learning: Evidence from high school mathematics.” PNAS, 2025
• Kosmyna et al., “Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of
Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing
Task.” arXiv preprint 2506.08872
• Stadler et al., “Cognitive ease at a cost: LLMs reduce mental
effort but compromise depth in student scientific inquiry.”
Computers in Human Behavior, 2024.
Question depth varies across courses, and surface
fluency can hide shallow learning.
Bastani et al. (2025); Kosmyna et al. (2025); Stadler et al. (2024); Tao, Mathematics in the Age of AI (2026)

slides.title: Why assisted learning can miss the learning goal
slides.navigationLabel: Why assisted learning can miss the learning goal
slides.text:
1 · WHY CHANGE 03b
Why assisted learning can miss the learning goal
Most observed questions are surface questions
Translation, explanation, summarize/quick-learn, and answer-course-test-question requests dominate the
observed interactions.
Possible explanations
1 · Incorrect use of AI
Lack of active retrieval and productive struggle.
2 · Partial assessments
Current assessments cannot fully assess capabilities
developed by AI-assisted learning, such as system
thinking and dealing with complexities.
TDAA question-depth coding; curriculum interpretation

TDAA: Learning and exploring in class
(3) TEST
Independent check
30 min · no AI

slides.title: The test anchors mastery without limiting exploration
slides.navigationLabel: The test anchors mastery without limiting exploration
slides.source: TDAA v1 course design; FCES 2026 deck
slides.text:
2 · TDAA 06
The test anchors mastery without limiting exploration
1. Reduce procrastination. Key for courses that have deep dependency.
2. Reward internalization. Sense of achievement.
3. Test core understanding. Questions target the average expected level; exploration is not
examined.
4. Leave room to explore. 120/130 points on paper, but capped at 100.
TDAA v1 course design; FCES 2026 deck

slides.title: The importance of the instructor
slides.text:
2 · TDAA 08
The importance of the instructor
Offline
1. Architect the learning
2. Generate learning materials
3. Prepare and collect good questions
Online
1. Support the learner mentally. Notice frustration, restore
confidence, and sustain motivation.
2. Guide learning and exploration. Check understanding,
give suggestions, answer and solicit questions.
3. Read the room. Decide when to intervene with a mini-
lecture, discussion, or student sharing.
💡 The instructor is the composer and conductor; let the class be water.
TDAA instructor role; course-design interpretation

slides.title: The importance of the instructor
slides.text:
2 · TDAA 08b
The importance of the instructor
Why will a student want to learn something hard?
1. Love the teacher (their passion for knowledge)
2. Has an interest in the course content
3. Has a need that the course can (partially) fulfill
4. Has a plan/dream
💡 The instructor is the key — they can influence all four fundamental motivations.
Adapted from Principal Rui BAO

slides.title: On exploration: teaching takes more preparation
slides.navigationLabel: On exploration: teaching takes more preparation
slides.source: Illustrative proof paths for uniqueness of reduced row echelon form; questions from learning and exploration
slides.text:
2 · TDAA 09
On exploration: teaching takes more preparation
AI or AI-assisted students can raise questions beyond the textbook. Instructors need full-stack
knowledge, preparation, and on-the-fly learning with AI.
Diverse perspective/routes
Proof of RREF’s uniqueness:
1. Construct the canonical form from the row
space (textbook).
2. Assume two different reduced forms; derive a
contradiction (student).
3. Use a dual-basis perspective (AI under
prompting).
Great questions
• Why does the Halting Problem proof not
apply to the halting problem for DFAs?
• A probability space has disjoint outcomes.
How should we model people’s menu choices?
• When extending a finite-class PAC bound to
an infinite class, can the growth function
Π(ℱ︀) replace ℋ︀, rather than using
Rademacher complexities?
💡 An underprepared or passive instructor may reasonably appear less helpful than AI.
Illustrative proof paths for uniqueness of reduced row echelon form; questions from learning and exploration

slides.title: DFS-style Learning
slides.source: Illustrative first-principles curriculum path; increase in abstraction levels
slides.text:
3 · THREE THESES 12
DFS-style Learning
Bound the probability of some rare event (typically |𝑋 − 𝔼[𝑋]|)
1 · CLT
Asymptotic bound
2 · Tail inequalities
Markov, Chebyshev, Hoeffding
3 · Extend the proof technique
(Upper) bound 𝑝(𝑥) ⟹ optimization problem
4 · Experiment
(Numerically) find the worst-case for a tight bound
Deeper: D. Bertsimas, I. Popescu. “Optimal Inequalities in Probability Theory: A Convex Optimization Approach.”, SIAM Journal
on Optimization, 2005.
💡 This is depth-first learning, or mini-research (enabled by AI): solve a real question, learn the needed tools,
explore in depth and make associations; periodically patch and consolidate.
Illustrative first-principles curriculum path; increase in abstraction levels

slides.title: Extremely personalized learning
slides.source: Personalized learning as a reinforcement-learning-style control loop
slides.text:
3 · THREE THESES 13
Extremely personalized learning
personalization becomes a control loop, not a topic label
fine-grained trace
attempts, errors, questions learner state
reasoning, effort, response
next action
material, exercise, schedule
reward
extrinsic (passive + proactive) + intrinsic
learning step
Reinforcement-learning-style learning
• State: reasoning, effort, and response.
• Trace: attempts, wrong steps, rereading,
questions, and feedback responses.
• Next action: material, exercise, depth, and
timing based on current evidence.
• Reward: based on the trace, next action, and
state; combine progress, AI feedback, and
curiosity.
💡 The current learning system is inefficient; choose a locally optimal policy to improve learning efficiency
significantly.
Personalized learning as a reinforcement-learning-style control loop

slides.title: Conclusions
slides.source: Design agenda; TDAA is a course experiment, not a verified system-wide gain
slides.text:
4 · INVITATION 14
Conclusions
AI changes both how students learn and what they need to learn.
Scientific research into AI + education
• Exploit AI’s capabilities, while keeping the learner’s reasoning visible.
• Understand and model how people learn, struggle, and transfer.
• Use technical and scientific methods: build, compare, measure, falsify.
• Develop and iterate quickly as the models change.
💡 Call for motivated instructors to join us to try out new ideas in real courses.
Design agenda; TDAA is a course experiment, not a verified system-wide gain
